content.p: On Monday 31 August 2026 a jury in Las Vegas found Duane "Keffe D" Davis guilty of murder with use of a deadly weapon in the 1996 killing of the rapper Tupac Shakur. Davis, 63, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, had pleaded not guilty. The jury of 12, sitting with four alternates, deliberated for less than three hours after a trial that lasted weeks. Prosecutors did not say Davis fired the shots. Their case was that he obtained a gun and called for the shooting, and that his own repeated words proved it.

The case is not finished. Judge Carli Kierny has scheduled sentencing for 13 October 2026 and ordered Davis held without bail until then. He faces up to life in prison. After the verdict he told the court he planned to appeal, and the judge answered that any appeal "happens after sentencing", according to Rolling Stone.
content.h2: The shooting the jury was asked about
content.p: On 7 September 1996 Shakur was in a black BMW driven by Marion "Suge" Knight, head of Death Row Records, when a white Cadillac pulled up beside it near the Las Vegas Strip and someone opened fire. Shakur died six days later at 25. Knight was grazed and survived. For years nobody was charged. Davis is the only man charged in the killing, according to Fox 11 and Fox 5.

The prosecution story begins a few hours earlier. After a Mike Tyson fight, Shakur and members of his entourage attacked Davis's nephew, Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, inside the MGM Grand casino, prosecutors said. Palal told jurors the shooting was gang retaliation for that beating. Anderson belonged to the South Side Compton Crips, while Knight's Death Row circle included members of the rival Mob Piru Bloods. Jurors heard that Trevon Lane, a Death Row associate, had spotted Anderson in the casino, and that a Death Row medallion chain had allegedly been snatched in a scuffle at a mall near Compton about two months before. Davis was at the fight but not in the brawl, the Associated Press reported.

Las Vegas police searched a Henderson home tied to Davis in July 2023 and took computers, a phone, a hard drive, several bullets, photographs and a copy of his memoir, according to the warrant described by NPR. On 29 September 2023 Davis was arrested on a walk near his home, and prosecutors announced that a grand jury had indicted him. DiGiacomo called him the "on-ground, on-site commander" who "ordered the death" of Shakur.

The case rested on what Davis had said himself. Retired LAPD detective Greg Kading told NPR that before Davis's public statements the cases were "unprosecutable as they stood". Anderson, long suspected of firing the shots, denied involvement and was killed in an unrelated shooting in Compton in 1998 at age 23. The other two men prosecutors placed in the Cadillac, DeAndre "Dre" Smith and Terrence "Bubble Up" Brown, are also dead, Rolling Stone reported.

The centrepiece was a recorded interview from 18 December 2008. LAPD detectives Kading and Daryn Dupree had gone to Davis's home in Corona, California, while looking into the 1997 killing of the rapper Christopher Wallace, known as the Notorious B.I.G., and into drug trafficking that could have sent Davis to prison. Dupree testified that Davis denied any part in the Wallace shooting, then said, "We did the other one." Davis then sat down for what is commonly called a "queen for a day" proffer session, with limited protections for what he said.

In the recording played to jurors he said he sat in the front passenger seat of the Cadillac, with Anderson behind him, Smith behind the driver and Brown at the wheel. He said his line of fire was blocked, so he handed a loaded Glock pistol back to the rear seat; Smith hesitated, and Anderson grabbed it and fired. "If we would have been on my side, I would have blasted," he said. Dupree testified that he believed Davis because Davis put the gun in his own nephew's hand.

The detectives told Davis that what he said could not be used against him. Prosecutors argued that Davis lost those protections by later repeating the details publicly, in a BET docuseries and in his 2019 memoir, "Compton Street Legend". DiGiacomo told jurors Davis did so because he was angry that Kading had written his own book. In 2009 Davis became a confidential informant, Dupree testified, and travelled to New York with investigators in an effort to reconnect with a man he identified as his link to Sean "Diddy" Combs. Combs has long denied any involvement, according to Fox 5 Las Vegas.

Jury selection began on 10 August 2026 from an initial pool of 75, with Judge Kierny warning of a trial of about five weeks. On the first day Davis waived his right to have the jury recommend a sentence, so there was no penalty phase and sentencing was left to the judge. Opening statements came on 17 August. Palal called the shooting an "act of revenge" amid tension between the Crips and the Mob Piru Bloods.

Prosecution witnesses included retired Las Vegas detective Brent Becker, who testified that witnesses behind the BMW described a white Cadillac with two to four people inside, that forensic testing pointed to a Glock pistol as the likely weapon, and that no witness could identify the shooter and no photo lineup produced an identification. A former Las Vegas officer, Garry Dale, said that in the ambulance he pressed the wounded Shakur again and again to name his attacker, and that Shakur refused. Reggie Wright Jr., who ran security for Death Row, described the rivalry between Knight's label and Combs's Bad Boy Records, and Denvonta Lee, an admitted Crips member, testified under a court order about the earlier mall brawl.

Jurors also heard about the Wallace investigation. Davis had been at the party Wallace was leaving when he was shot and drove an Impala, so he was briefly scrutinised. Jurors were told that neither the court nor the LAPD believes he was involved in that killing. A former LAPD detective, Fred Miller, agreed on cross-examination that he was not aware of evidence Davis was actually owed money by Combs or Wallace.

Knight, serving a 28-year California sentence for running over and killing a Compton businessman in 2015, had said he would not testify. He and several others on the prosecution's witness list, including former Las Vegas mayor Oscar Goodman, Joe Lombardo, the former sheriff who is now Nevada's governor and Kading, were never called. Prosecutors rested on Wednesday 26 August, after eight days of witnesses and hours of recordings.

Sanft's argument, from his opening statement to his closing, was that Davis's accounts were stories told for leverage and money. He said Davis invented the 2008 account to gain leverage in the drug investigation and repeated it later for profit, and he told jurors authorities knew Davis was "full of crap" and did not corroborate it. He pointed to a memoir passage saying a Chrysler Sebring full of women was hit by gunfire; a woman from that car testified it was never struck. "We can't put Orlando in the car. We can't even put Davis in Las Vegas," he told jurors in closing.

The defence called three witnesses on 27 August, all former police. Two former Las Vegas officers, Sgt. Stan Hyt and Lt. Charlie Mangrum, said they saw a light-coloured Cadillac at Knight's house that night. The third, Det. Dan Long, led the Shakur investigation from 2002 to 2017. He said that after a 2009 interview with Davis he wanted to seek a murder arrest warrant but was later told to "stand down", apparently because of the proffer agreement, and that some of his reports were lost when the department changed storage systems. Davis did not testify.

Palal told jurors the case was "drenched with circumstantial evidence" even without Davis's confessions, and that for nearly 18 years Davis had told police, television and interviewers he was responsible. "Tell him you hear him. Find him guilty," he said. DiGiacomo, in rebuttal, held up Davis's scrapbook of articles about Shakur: "This guy's scrapbooking his murder." He admitted that Las Vegas authorities "had to eat crow" and let Davis live in Henderson uncharged for years. Sanft asked why, if Davis had truly confessed, the case was being tried 30 years later, and said the state had no phone records or other physical evidence showing Davis was the shot caller.

The jury began deliberating on the afternoon of 31 August and returned within three hours. Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, cried and hugged the prosecutors. The Shakur family called itself "elated and relieved" in a statement. Prosecutors declined to comment, and the family said it would wait until sentencing.

Sentencing on 13 October is the next fixed event, and because Davis waived a jury sentence, the judge alone will decide it. Reports differ on the precise charge. Good Morning America and Variety said the guilty verdict was for murder with a deadly weapon plus the gang-intent language; the Associated Press said prosecutors would drop a gang enhancement for reasons of witness logistics, and reported a conviction on a single count of murder with a deadly weapon. Rolling Stone said Davis faces up to life without the possibility of parole, while other outlets said up to life. The judge told Davis an appeal "happens after sentencing". The Notorious B.I.G.'s killing in 1997 remains unsolved, according to the Associated Press.
